blocks.x: A real one, December 15, 1961. We're recording today at French Market Fisherman Supplies, 813 Decatur Street. What's your name? Paul Crawford. And mine's Dick Allen. We're waiting on Albert Artighe. He's talking to young Louis Armstrong downstairs, a trumpet player who happens to have the same name as the original Louis Armstrong. While it's fresh in my mind, I thought I'd add that young Louis Armstrong says he's some sort of little off cousin to the original Louis Armstrong. Says that when he first got started, he played some with George Lewis. He had an old man, I believe it was Armstrong's band, not George Lewis's, had an old man called Kaiser, John Joseph's brother, Willie Joseph, also in the band. And when he was young, what is that, about 14 or 16? 14 I believe it was. He talked to Elmer Talbot. We sent him to see Professor Pritchett, who was loaded, he said. I presume he meant that he was full of students. And Pritchett's University Professor Delmont, who taught him. First thing I want to know is your name. Albert Artighe. That's with a S on the end? Yeah. A-R-T-I-G-U-E-S. Mm-hmm. I see. Now the embarrassing questions. When were you born?

August 23rd, 1907. And where were you born? The house I'm living in now, 2733 Demain Street. Never have moved. Did it belong to your family? My dad built it a year before I was born. Did your dad or your
uncle or grandfather, anybody play music? Nobody in the family played music. I'm the only one in the family. How in the world did you ever get interested?

I don't know. I just saw a horn and liked it, picked it up. I was going to Holy Cross College at the time and got planted by ear. Never did. No, I started to take a few lessons at school. And I wanted to play Dixieland music and the brother wanted me to play march music. So it didn't jive. I quit the class real soon and got to playing by ear, you know. And I formed my own band. After a while I went with Joe Kless's band. From there, Sharky left to go with the Wolverines in New York and Norman Brownlee took me to take his place with Norman Brownlee's band. But I never had any lessons. I just more or less picked what I didn't learn up from Sharky himself. I used to go sit in with him at the, when the Taunty was running Sharky, was the right young fella himself then. He's about ten years older than me. Sharky's about
sixty-three, sixty-four. Before you started playing, did you listen to many bands before

you ever touched a horn? Oh yeah, I heard quite a few Dixieland bands. In those days they had all these good colored bands around town. Chris Kelly, Punch, Rene, Papa Celestine, they were all young comers then, you know what I mean? And they all played a powerful lot of music. Buddy Petit played nice stuff those days. Punch, Sam Morgan, Chris Kelly. Oh and they had quite a few good white bands. Pansaline had a good white Dixieland band. Johnny Beisdorff was at his peak. He was playing the Tokyo Gardens out at the Spanish Fort and Papa Celestine had the original tuxedos right across from him, the tranchinas. He had a good outfit. What's a king cake party? King cake party, he used to give these parties where they have a little doll or pecan in the cake. And whoever got that pecan had to give a party the following week. It would start around, I think, January or February the 8th. And it would go on for a couple of three weeks, or maybe four weeks, until somebody had got the pecan and didn't throw a party. Then the king cake party automatically peed it out. And what would they have at these parties? Well they'd have a beer, whiskey, stuff to drink, and a band. Nine out of ten the band got mule, because those people didn't have a lot of money those days. They'd hire a band for around eighteen dollars. And Kid Punch would come out there and they'd get Punch or Rene or whoever was playing good and loaded. When it come for time to pay the band off, whoever drew the party was hard to find. They were gone.
What is this, Mule? What is this, Mule?

What is this, Mule? What is this? Mule? What is this? Mule? What would they have at these parties? Well they'd have a beer, whiskey, stuff to drink, and a band. Nine out of ten the band got mule, because those people didn't have a lot of money those days. They'd hire a band for around eighteen dollars. And Kid Punch would come out there and they'd get Punch or Rene or whoever was playing good and loaded. They'd come for time to pay the band off, whoever drew the party was hard to find. They were gone. What is this, Mule, you say? Yeah, put the mule on them, wouldn't pay them, you know. I see. And they half expected it, I tell you the truth. Kid Punch and Rene, Sam Morgan, those fellas, they half expected to be mule. And these fellas, some of them would be nervous enough to hide two bands for the party, you know, let them buck one.
Did you ever hear any good contests like that? Oh, I did.

Man, I heard some contests out of this world, especially when they had all those camps at West End. The Lillian Cottage, the Dixie Cottage, American Club. And man, they'd come out on the wharf, the trumpet men would come out on the wharf. The camps had big long wharfs leading to them, you know. They'd come out there and blow at one another. I even got tied up in some of them duels myself. We used to play a lot at the Lillian Cottage out at West End. And those bands would come in the American Club or the Norma Villa, right near there. You couldn't help with getting a duel because once you'd start playing, they'd try to come out on the wharf and play at you. That was something, man. For a dollar, you could go out there on a Saturday evening with your girl if you wanted, eat and drink all Saturday night and dancing from 9 to 6 Sunday for a dollar.
A dollar and a couple. Nine to six, that's six o'clock at night?

All day, all day. From nine to morning, six at night. What paid for all that, Dick, they used to put out an ad card and then take it around to the business people and get a five or ten dollar ad. Well, before they threw the picnic, everything was paid for. The band, the eats, the liquor, whatever they had was paid for. And what would they do with these cards? Well, they'd just put them around town as advertisements, see.
They'd have the advertisement for the picnic and for the...
That's right. The place of business would have a spot, whatever they bought. Two dollars spot, five dollars spot, ten dollars spot. And then they'd place them around town as advertisements.
Well, that was worth it to them, I guess, too. It worked out fine.

It worked out fine for everybody. It worked out fine for the people giving the picnic. They'd pay for everything. And what they got took in, these dollars they took in, was all great. They had card paid for the paying and the eats. And whatever they took in in the admissions was great. And they had them, oh man, they had three or four of them on a Sunday. Mellon Boyd was a hot spot for all their paintings.
Who did you buck against?

Oh, I bucked against Pant Hook Lane, even Punch. I played against Punch, Rene. They used to come out there and they'd be... You couldn't help it. You'd be playing the dancers and they'd come in and play right next to you.
How did that feel when you were bucking against those guys?

Well, they'd just make you blow your heart out, Dick, that's all. I've seen myself blow so much, split my lip wide open. Just trying to hit them high notes at them, you know. And that's what the whole thing was. They'd just see who could out blow the other fella. And man, that music in those tin roof camps really sound nice. Incidentally, I played a job about five years ago on the 4th of July with Johnny McGee. He played with me and old Bill Wally was with us. We had a five piece combo. Talk about sounding nice, Dick. At Lil Woods. Not Lil Woods, between Lil Woods and the airport. One of those camps.
Around them Mommaloos in that area?

That's right. And we had Bill on bass, myself on trumpet, Johnny McGee playing clarinet, Tony Shrine on drums, and Sam Callie on guitar. You ever hear him play guitar? I think a long time ago with you. Oh man, he sounds like a piano man on a guitar. You don't need a piano, Paul, when you play with him. Really nice. He still plays nice.

Is it Gene Hemard or what is his name, Hemard? Gene Ory or whatever he tells himself he used to play with you some? He played guitar. I think he played with you or Red Hot. Maybe I got it confused. He played with Red Hot.

No, the only guitar man I played with was Lil Durfee. Durfee, that's years ago. I played with a little man. His brother played clarinet, he played guitar, Cat's Mastry played drum. I used to play trumpet.
What's his brother's name? Durfee, Frank Durfee. Frank Durfee is a guitar player? And which, wait a minute, I can't get this straight.

I can't remember whether Frank, no, Frank's brother played guitar. Frank was clarinet. I forget his brother's name. I can't remember. That's been many years ago. That's when I first started. I did. That's when we used to play Fireman's Hole over in Wiggle.
Yeah, we were just talking to Lil Armstrong about that. That's right.

Said he played over there. I used to play over there with Brownlee too at Thomas East, right out of Harvey. Every Saturday night. You talk about a hot spot. That was it. And we used to play at the Red Top Inn in Gretchen. That was a bar with Brownlee. We'd come back sometime after the Thomas East would break up with Gil going in. Played just with the bars, you know. This Norman Brownlee was a regular guy.
Do you know him, Dan? Yeah, I know him. I went to Pensacola.

Fine, fine. He's very nice. Yeah. And he was a good counterman. Still is. I'm hurting him lately. He sat down with Raymond and me when we were there with Al Marico in 1958. Came in. He still sure plays good. Yeah, he used to be. Well he played a lead piano. One of the few lead pianos I ever played with, Paul. He knew tempos and when he'd set a tempo, man it was wonderful.
What's a lead piano?
Well, a lead would take off and set the tempo for you, Dick.
He'd play the first chorus or something?
Play the introduction and the number, you know. And bring you right into the key you're going in and set the tempo for you. And then the trumpet man would take you from there.
What did he play in the ensemble?

Well he played chords after he took off. Yeah, after that. He didn't continue playing the lead like some guys did. No, no, no. Just a take off man. They call him a lead or take off man. Now Sam Cagliar can do the same thing with a guitar. I'm telling you, take off man, set a tempo for you that you're just as relaxed. You ought to hear that guy play, Dick.
I haven't heard him in a long time. I didn't know I used to hear him. That is nice. What was it, Magazine in Peniston? Yeah, he used to play up there, that's right.
What's the name of that?
Charlie's Tavern or something I think. Something damn fun though.
I played up there.
They changed it to the Elm Bowl Room. They keep changing the name of that place.
I saw you up there one night. Yeah.
We took some pictures, remember? Yeah. And all that, uh, Ralston Crawford, the red-faced photographer. From New York. Yeah.
I was playing with, that was, uh, McGee's man up there.
Is Johnny in the Union now? I don't know.
I haven't seen Johnny in, oh God knows when, Dick.

I saw him a few months ago. He was at Tulane. I didn't know what the hell he was. He's a fine boy. He is. Uh, when you started out on trumpet, did you sit in any before you ever began to come professional?

Oh yeah. I sat in with quite a few bands. Dick, I sat in with Pinky. When Pinky was with the Owls. I used to go around. Well in those days you could sit, nobody was Union, sit in with anybody, you know? I used to always, wherever Sharky played I'd be, when I was a youngster. And, uh, sitting with Sharky, Sharky let me, you know, take down and let me do most of the driving. He used to get a kick out of me because I was about, oh I was only about sixteen years old, just a youngster.
Did you model your playing on anybody in those days in particular?

No, I just played from my heart, Dick. I still do. When I play I don't try to imitate anybody. I just play the way I feel. And the more relaxed a group is that I'm with, the better I feel about it. I don't like to have to extend myself to keep up with a group. I like to play relaxed music. Well what makes it relaxed? Well you just play what you feel, Dick. When you get to the point where you're extending yourself to reach notes, it's no longer relaxed. And then it gets to be work. You know what I mean, Paul? When you've got to extend yourself to reach them high notes and make, put so much stuff, I tell you I see a lot of good men that play good Dickson and music. They go modern, you know what I mean? And they try to put so much in the damn room until it just confuses their style. They don't sound good anymore. What about tempo? Well that's very essential. The tempo is very essential. If you don't have tempo you don't have anything.
What's the fastest you like to play? Could you just clap it with your hands or beat it with your feet?
Well I don't go very much for fast music unless it's a standard that has to be played fast, like Tiger Rag or some standard that was written fast. But I like a two beat tempo, it's relaxed.
What tempo do you like Tiger Rag in for example? Well...

Well I always did like to, Dick. I always, whenever I knew a voice of a tune, I always liked to play the last two boys, start the voice and then go into the chorus.
